analysis.one_liner: Bans 'forever chemicals' (PFAS) intentionally added to cosmetics.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to a House committee, never received a markup or a floor vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Department of Health and Human Services to write and finalize a rule banning the intentional addition of PFAS — long-lasting synthetic chemicals sometimes used to make cosmetics waterproof or long-wearing — from makeup and other personal care products. It had bipartisan support but was never taken up by the committee it was sent to.
analysis.who_benefits: People who use cosmetics would be protected from skin exposure to PFAS, chemicals that persist in the body and the environment and have been linked in scientific studies to health harms. A federal ban would also spare state regulators from writing a patchwork of differing rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People who wear makeup and skincare

how_it_helps.text: Requires HHS to issue a proposed rule within 270 days and finalize it within 90 days after that, banning intentionally added PFAS from cosmetics [S3].
PFAS are man-made chemicals with fully fluorinated carbon atoms that persist in the environment and the body; the bill covers any such substance added on purpose [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Cosmetics and personal care manufacturers would bear the cost of removing PFAS from their formulas and retesting products, and the suppliers of PFAS ingredients for cosmetics would lose that market.

drawbacks.text: The compliance timeline is fast: a proposed rule within 270 days and a final rule 90 days later gives industry limited runway to reformulate and retest products [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge that the health risk from PFAS in a cosmetic product applied to skin may be smaller than from contaminated drinking water, though the chemicals accumulate and a ban removes exposure at the source.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — eliminating avoidable exposure to persistent chemicals through products applied directly to the skin — outweighs the cost of reformulation, which some large manufacturers have already made for some products. The main weakness is the tight rulemaking timetable, a design detail, not a reason the bill died.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee, sat there for the rest of the Congress, and expired in January 2023 without a committee vote or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Debbie Dingell introduced the bill on June 17, 2021, joined by Reps. Kuster, Fitzpatrick, and Katko — a bipartisan group [S3].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and the next day to that committee's Health Subcommittee [S5].
No further action appears in the record: no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote, in the roughly 18 months remaining in the 117th Congress [S5].
It drew 17 cosponsors, 15 Democrats and 2 Republicans [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cosmetics and personal care manufacturers are better off: they avoided a federal ban on PFAS in their products and kept the option to use those ingredients. People who use cosmetics gained nothing from the bill's death beyond continued voluntary industry practices.

for.name: Rep. Debbie Dingell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban intentionally added PFAS in cosmetics

for.name: Reps. Ann Kuster, Brian Fitzpatrick, and John Katko
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors, giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship from the start

against.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or brought it to the floor; the bill sat in committee and died at the end of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: The bill itself was bipartisan — 15 Democratic and 2 Republican cosponsors — and its death was not a roll-call defeat but a decision not to act on it.

industries.note: PFAS help some products resist water and wear, so a ban would force reformulation and product retesting. Industry's interest in keeping the ingredients runs against consumers' interest in avoiding exposure to persistent chemicals.
Companies selling PFAS for cosmetic use would lose that market. Their interest in continued sales runs against the public's interest in reduced exposure.
